attested {{Circa|1780}} | ref = | familycolor = arawakan | fam1 = [[Maipurean languages|Arawakan]] | fam2 = Northern | fam3 = [[Upper Amazon Arawakan|Upper Amazonian]] | fam4 = Orinoco | fam5 = Yavitero languages | iso3 = bvv | glotto = bani1254 | glottorefname = Avane | era = | dia1 = Quirruba | dia2 = Baniva-Avani | altname = Baniwa, Abane }} '''Avane''' ('''Abane'''), one of several languages called '''Baniwa''', also known as '''Baniva Yavitero,'''{{Cite web|url=https://www.ethnologue.com/language/bvv|title=Baniva|website=Ethnologue|language=en|access-date=2019-09-20|archive-date=2019-07-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190703205755/https://www.ethnologue.com/language/bvv|url-status=live}} was an [[Arawakan language]] of [[Venezuela]]. It is believed to have become [[Extinct language|extinct]] by the late 20th century, and is only attested in a short word-list from the late 18th century. == History == It was primarily spoken in the [[Amazonas (Venezuelan state)|Amazonas]] region of Venezuela and along the [[Colombia]]n border, and had dialects called '''Quirruba''' and '''Baniva-Avani'''.{{Cite web|url=https://glottolog.org/resource/languoid/id/bani1254|title=Glottolog 4.0 - Avane|website=glottolog.org|access-date=2019-09-20|archive-date=2019-09-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190920204945/https://glottolog.org/resource/languoid/id/bani1254|url-status=live}} The language likely began deteriorating with the arrival of the Jesuits in the late 18th century. The Avane language included a colloquial name to refer to the neighboring indigenous Maipure people, {{lang|bvv|Metimetichini}}, which may be humorously alluding to the polysyllabic nature of many [[Maipure language|Maipure words]] and contains two sounds not usually found in Avane.{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/zamponi-maipure_2003|title=Maipure|last=Zamponi|first=Raoul|publisher=Lincom|year=2003|location=Munich}} The language also shares some words with others in the same family, including Maipure and [[Guipunave]], but is clearly phonetically distinct. == Phonology == Avane is characterized phonetically in comparison to Maipure, showing some large differences. Avane uses the [[dental stop]] [d], which is not seen in Maipure but is native to Yavitero and Baniva. It uses the [[glottal fricative]] [h] ([x]) before [i] and/or [a], where Maipure would use [t], [k], and [j]. Also unlike Maipure, the Avane [[diphthong]]s [ai] and [au] do not appear to be contracted in [[stressed syllable]]s. Ethnographer [[Filippo Salvatore Gilii|Gilij]] described the Avane pronunciation as "rude, guttural" compared to the Maipure's "gentle, beautiful" version.{{Cite book|title=American Indian languages : the historical linguistics of Native America|last=Campbell|first=Lyle|date = 21 September 2000|isbn=9780195349832|location=Oxford|oclc=1108851780}} == Morphology == In morphology, Avane is seen as close to Maipure, with both using the "empty morph" [[suffix]] "{{lang|bvv|-cà}}" for certain [[Active verb|active]] and mainly [[Intransitive verb|intransitive]] verbs. == Vocabulary == {| class="wikitable" |+Attested Avane words !Avane !Gloss |- |{{lang|bvv|javaxì}} |axe |- |{{lang|bvv|pussi}} |manioc bread |- |{{lang|bvv|casimeje}} |a dance |- |{{lang|bvv|Diòsu}} |God |- |{{lang|bvv|ada}} |grater |- |{{lang|bvv|tamàu}} |he went |- |{{lang|bvv|nuxa}} |I |- |{{lang|bvv|nuxacàu}} |I go |- |{{lang|bvv|nujutuà}} |I smoke |- |{{lang|bvv|quaxixì}} ({{lang|bvv|quajijì}}) |jaguar |- |{{lang|bvv|Metimetichinì}} |Maipure |- |{{lang|bvv|napài}} |my father |- |{{lang|bvv|unè}} |skin disease |- |{{lang|bvv|Purrùnaminàri}} |supreme being |- |{{lang|bvv|yema}} |tobacco |- |{{lang|bvv|inioxì}} |woman |- |{{lang|bvv|saje}}, {{lang|bvv|ja}} |yes |} ==References== {{Reflist}} {{Arawakan languages}} [[Category:Indigenous languages of the South American Northern Foothills]] [[Category:Arawakan languages]] [[Category:Extinct languages of South America]] [[Category:Languages of Venezuela]]
